strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the safety-utility trade-off in activation steering for LLM refusal is important and the paper positions itself well against vector calibration and conditional steering approaches.

Principled and clean formulation: constraining the steering matrix to the null space of benign activations plus closed-form regularized least-squares for refusal direction reconstruction is simple, computationally efficient (via the Lemma 1 covariance equivalence), and well-justified with complete proofs in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three LLM backbones, seven diverse jailbreak attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, Cipher, GCG, Jailbroken, PAIR, ReNeLLM), four utility benchmarks, three recent steering baselines, and an RV ablation that cleanly isolates the trade-off. AlphaSteer achieves high DSR (91-98% avg) while matching vanilla utility, a convincing result.

Good mechanism analysis: PCA visualizations, L2 norm distributions of steering vectors, and steering-strength sweeps (RQ2) provide evidence for *why* the method preserves utility, not just that it does; extensive appendix covers eigenvalue distributions, hyperparameter selection, and case studies.
Responsible disclosure practices: warning about harmful content, GPT-4o evaluation prompts released, broader impacts section including discussion of potential backdoor misuse.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the null-space projection machinery is directly borrowed from prior work (AlphaEdit, null-space continual learning), and the safety component is essentially ridge regression toward a fixed refusal vector. The 'theoretically grounded' framing is somewhat oversold - the underlying lemmas are straightforward linear algebra, and the method implicitly relies on the same benign/malicious separability assumption as the conditional-steering baselines it criticizes for lacking theory.

No evaluation against adaptive or defense-aware attacks. Since AlphaSteer is essentially a learned linear gate on activations, a natural question is whether attackers aware of the defense can craft jailbreaks that lie in (or near) the benign null space; the paper evaluates only static attacks, so claims of robustness are not fully supported.

Evaluation scale is modest: the test set is 100 AdvBench prompts per attack, GPT-4o as sole judge (no human verification or agreement statistics reported), and utility benchmarks are subsampled to 100 questions. Results may not be statistically robust; no variance or significance reporting.

Several design choices appear empirically tuned and under-justified: the null-space threshold p%, regularization alpha, layer selection based on 'observation on separability', and model-specific lambda values. It is unclear on which data these were tuned (potential leakage with the test set), and sensitivity analysis for p% and alpha is relegated to visual inspection.

Missing comparisons with non-steering defense baselines (e.g., input perturbation, Circuit Breaker-style approaches, safety decoders) and no evaluation on larger or differently sized models; the limitations section acknowledges only the model-size issue.

The utility score aggregation and the weighting across the four benchmarks are not precisely defined, making Table 2 harder to interpret, and only average DSR differences (not per-attack variance) are discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: the safety-utility trade-off in activation steering for LLM jailbreak defense. The motivation and problem framing are clear and easy to follow.

The proposed method is simple, training-free at inference, and has a closed-form solution (regularized least squares), making it computationally cheap. The null-space projection for utility preservation is an elegant mechanism borrowed from prior work.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: three LLM backbones, seven jailbreak attacks, and four utility benchmarks, with consistent gains over three steering baselines (Jailbreak Antidote, Surgical, CAST) on both defense success rate and utility preservation.

The mechanistic analysis (PCA visualizations of benign vs. malicious activations, L2 norm distributions of steering vectors, effect of steering strength lambda) provides useful insight into why the method preserves benign activations while steering malicious ones.

Implementation details, hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and dataset construction are documented in the appendix, supporting reproducibility; code release is promised. A dual-use risk discussion is included.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core technical ingredient (null-space projection for constraining weight modifications to preserve certain behaviors) is directly imported from AlphaEdit (Fang et al., ICLR 2025) and null-space continual learning; the safety-enhancement step is standard ridge regression mapping activations to a diff-in-means refusal vector. The contribution is an application of existing tools to a new problem rather than a new principled framework, making the repeated claims of being 'theoretically grounded' overstated.

The theory does not actually support the central claim of generalization. Delta h_b = 0 is guaranteed only for activations in the training benign set (and, due to the p% eigenvalue truncation, the retained subspace is not a true null space even for those). For unseen benign prompts and unseen jailbreak attacks, there is no guarantee that benign activations are untouched or that malicious activations map to r. The paper's 'theoretical grounding' narrative oversells what is essentially an in-sample least-squares fit.

Despite criticizing prior methods as heuristic, the method itself introduces several heuristic choices: the p% eigenvalue truncation threshold, selection of middle layers based on visual separability of steering-vector norms, and per-model lambda (0.5, 0.45, 0.14) with no systematic selection procedure or ablation of these choices in the main text. This weakens the positioning against the baselines.

Evaluation robustness concerns: (1) test sets are only 100 prompts per attack; (2) DSR/CR are judged solely by GPT-4o with no human validation of judge reliability; (3) training data draws 720 prompts from AdvBench, the same source as the test questions, so distribution overlap between train and test remains despite deduplication; (4) no adaptive/white-box attack evaluation, even though the steering transformation is a deterministic linear map that an adaptive adversary could probe or evade - a standard requirement for defense papers.

Baseline fairness is unclear. No detail is given on how baseline hyperparameters (e.g., lambda ranges, thresholds) were tuned, while AlphaSteer's lambda is model-specific; the very poor CAST results (0% on math) could partly reflect suboptimal baseline configuration.

Limited scale and scope: only three ~7-9B models; no evaluation on larger models, other safety domains, or robustness to distribution shift. The limitations section acknowledges model scale but not the missing adaptive-attack or generalization analysis.

The utility guarantee is approximate in practice (e.g., XSTest compliance drops from 92.4 to 91.2 on Llama-3.1), yet the paper claims benign activations remain 'essentially unchanged'; a quantitative measure of activation drift on held-out benign data would strengthen the claim beyond PCA plots.
Writing quality is uneven: typos ('inlcude', 'suffer from degrade'), inconsistent notation in places, and some figures (e.g., dense appendix figure grids) are hard to read.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important problem (safety-utility trade-off in activation steering) with a principled formulation: null-space projection for utility preservation plus regularized least-squares reconstruction of refusal directions for safety enhancement, with a clean closed-form solution (Eq. 9).

The technical presentation is rigorous: proofs of the null-space equivalence lemma, projection guarantee, and closed-form solution are provided in the appendix, and the computational simplification via the covariance matrix is well motivated.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: three LLM backbones, seven diverse jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, ReNeLLM, Cipher, etc.), four utility benchmarks covering over-refusal, instruction following, and reasoning, plus the RV ablation that nicely quantifies the trade-off the method avoids.

The analysis (RQ2) is informative: activation dynamics visualization, L2-norm distribution of steering vectors for benign vs. malicious prompts, and the effect of steering strength λ support the claimed mechanism and strengthen the empirical case.
Deduplication of train/test prompts and explicit leakage controls are described, and the broader-impact discussion (potential misuse as a backdoor) is honest and appropriate.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core technique is a direct transfer of null-space projection ideas from prior work (AlphaEdit [30], null-space continual learning [29]) to activation steering, combined with standard ridge regression; the framing as 'learning' is somewhat overstated since the solution is a closed-form least-squares fit rather than an optimization over model behavior.

Hyperparameter and layer selection raise evaluation concerns: layers and the null-space threshold p% are chosen 'via our observation on the separability' of steering-vector norms (Appendix D.6), which risks selecting configurations on data correlated with the test distribution; no sensitivity study or principled selection procedure on held-out data is provided.

Evaluation scale and judging are modest: only 100 test prompts per attack and GPT-4o as sole judge (with no human validation or agreement statistics reported), which limits confidence in the large DSR margins; adaptive or white-box attacks specifically targeting the null-space steering are not considered.

The method implicitly relies on benign/malicious activations being separable with respect to the learned null space, i.e., it is effectively a linear discriminator; generalization to OOD jailbreak styles and adversarial manipulation of activations (which the linear structure invites) is untested.

Minor reproducibility and clarity issues: the code link in the abstract is empty ('available at .'), which conflicts with the reproducibility claims; there are typos/notation slips (e.g., 'd_model' vs. 'd' for ∆ dimensions, equation formatting errors in Eq. 8); and 'theoretical grounding' is modest—it is elementary linear algebra rather than a nontrivial guarantee.
Only linear transformation matrices are explored and only three ~7-9B models are tested; the limitations section concedes this, but it narrows the claimed significance of the contribution.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the safety–utility trade-off in activation steering is an important, timely issue, and the paper clearly identifies the mechanism by which indiscriminate steering harms benign prompts (Figure 1b PCA analysis).

Principled and clean methodology: constraining the transformation matrix to the null space of benign activations gives an exact, closed-form guarantee (ΔH_b = 0) for utility preservation, with complete proofs (Lemma 1, closed-form regularized least-squares solution in Appendix B), and a favorable computational cost analysis (Appendix C).

Comprehensive evaluation: 7 jailbreak attacks across 3 main LLMs plus additional model sizes (Llama-3.2-1B/3B), 4 utility benchmarks, comparisons against 4 representative baselines (Surgical, Jailbreak Antidote, CAST, Circuit Breaker) and refusal SFT, showing strong DSR improvements (91–98% avg) with near-vanilla utility.

Robustness and generalization analyses that go beyond typical evaluations: adaptive white-box GCG attack against the defense (95.5% DSR), unseen attack families (AdvPrompter, FlipAttack, WildGuard), OOD domain generalization (math data ablation with PEC coverage analysis), benign data-size ablation, null-space ratio ablation, and an MLP-vs-linear regression ablation.

Strong attention to evaluation validity: information-leakage checks via BLEU deduplication between train/test, comparison across two different evaluators (GPT-4o and Llama-Guard-3-8B) with an honest analysis of their disagreement, transparent GPT-4o judging prompts, and released anonymous code.
Well-written, clear presentation with informative figures linking activation-space geometry to model behavior (case studies, activation dynamics under varying steering strength).
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate/incremental: the core technique (null-space projection of a learned transformation, covariance-based efficient null-space computation, closed-form regression) is directly borrowed from AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025) and null-space continual learning (Wang et al., 2021); the contribution is primarily adapting this machinery to refusal steering rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The 'theoretically grounded' claim is somewhat overstated: the theory amounts to standard linear algebra (null-space equivalence, ridge regression closed form) and rests on an unproven assumption that malicious activations are linearly separable from the benign span. If a jailbreak's activations lie substantially inside the benign subspace, the steering vector vanishes exactly where defense is needed; only a limited adaptive-GCG study probes this vulnerability.

Layer selection, steering strength λ, and null-space ratio p are tuned per model based on norm-separability observations (Appendix F.9), which is itself a heuristic selection procedure, partially undercutting the critique of prior methods as 'heuristic'.

Train/test distributions for safety overlap: both the 720 training malicious prompts and the 100 test prompts come from AdvBench, plus shared sources like MaliciousInstruct/JBB; deduplication mitigates but does not eliminate distribution-shift concerns, and the 100-question test set per attack is small for reporting 1-point DSR differences without variance/confidence estimates.

Only 7–9B open-source models are evaluated; effectiveness on larger or reasoning models is unaddressed (acknowledged in limitations), and the method's reliance on a benign activation subspace may not scale cleanly to larger model families or to multi-turn/agentic settings.

Minor consistency issues: p ablation results are non-monotonic (p=0.9 yields higher DSR than the default p=0.6 with no explanation), and the α regularization hyperparameter's sensitivity is not reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem (the safety-utility trade-off in activation steering for LLM refusal) with a simple, closed-form, training-free solution that is computationally cheap (90s vs 20min for refusal SFT).

The empirical evaluation is broad: three main 7-9B models plus smaller models, seven jailbreak attacks plus additional OOD benchmarks (AdvPrompter, FlipAttack, WildGuardTest), utility benchmarks covering instruction following, over-refusal (XSTest), and math reasoning, and a comparison against refusal training and Circuit Breaker.

The core technical components (null-space projection, ridge regression to reconstruct the refusal direction) are clearly stated with complete derivations in the appendix, and the analysis of PEC/space coverage (Appendix F.7) is a genuinely useful contribution that connects utility degradation to benign-subspace coverage.

The paper includes several above-average robustness checks for this line of work: an adaptive white-box GCG attack against the steered system, an evaluation-model ablation (GPT-4o vs Llama-Guard), data-leakage analysis via BLEU similarity, and ablations on benign data size, null-space ratio p, and MLP vs linear head.
Reproducibility support is reasonable: anonymous code, detailed hyperparameters, evaluation prompts, and an ethics statement that acknowledges dual-use risks.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The method is essentially a composition of existing ingredients: null-space projection borrowed from AlphaEdit (Fang et al., 2025) and continual-learning null-space training (Wang et al., 2021), applied to ridge regression toward a diff-in-means refusal vector (Arditi et al., 2024). The framing of 'learnable activation steering' oversells what is a closed-form linear least-squares fit. The repeated claim of being 'theoretically grounded' is weakly supported: the null-space constraint guarantees zero steering only on the *training* benign activations; generalization to test activations is an empirical assumption (characterized only post-hoc via PEC), not a theoretical property.

Several results are internally inconsistent or insufficiently explained. On Llama-3.1-8B, AlphaSteer scores only 63% DSR on Cipher while the naive RV baseline achieves 100%, suggesting the null-space constraint actively blocks refusal for encoded attacks - a meaningful failure mode that is never analyzed. Table 16 shows non-monotonic DSR vs p (p=0.3 gives 92.37 vs 91.93 at p=0.6) despite the claimed 'clear upward trend', and Table 15 shows DSR *increasing* to 99.71 as benign training data shrinks to 1k, which contradicts the paper's own coverage narrative and hints the constraint is what limits refusal; this trade-off deserves analysis rather than presentation as supporting evidence.

Evaluation rigor is limited relative to the strength of the claims: only 100 harmful prompts per attack, a single GPT-4o judge (with known jailbreak-judgment brittleness), no variance/seed reporting, and small utility samples (100 questions from GSM8K/MATH500). Per-model steering strengths (λ = 0.5/0.45/0.14) and per-model layer choices are selected 'via our observation' - it is unclear whether these were tuned on validation or test data, which matters because the headline DSR numbers sit on a steep DSR-λ curve (Figure 4a).

The baselines comparison has fairness concerns: CAST is configured in a way that catastrophically fails on math (0% on GSM8K/MATH for all models), and the paper attributes this entirely to CAST's design, yet such a drastic collapse may reflect implementation/configuration rather than the method; the strong Circuit Breaker baseline is trained with LoRA under unclear matched-data conditions.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: dimensional notation is muddled (Δ ∈ R^{d×d_model} vs R^{d×d} used interchangeably; Hm projections written inconsistently as PĤm vs P̂Hm), Equation 20/22 contain formatting errors, duplicated citations (Zou et al. 2023b/c, Ouyang et al. 2022a/b, Han et al. 2024a/b), a wrong model name ('Llama-3.1-1B-Instruct' in Table 6 vs Llama-3.2-1B in Table 5), and a reference to 'Table 7' where Table 7/Figure 7 is meant in Appendix E.6.

Scope limitations are acknowledged only briefly: all experiments are on 1B-9B open models with greedy decoding; generalization to larger or reasoning models, and behavior under multi-turn or obfuscated attacks beyond the tested set, remain unknown. Given that the method's safety guarantee is distribution-dependent (subspace coverage), the practical robustness story is thinner than the abstract suggests.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (safety-utility trade-off in activation steering) with a clean, principled formulation: a null-space-constrained transformation matrix that yields near-zero steering for benign activations and refusal-direction reconstruction for malicious ones.

The methodology is technically sound and easy to follow; the closed-form solution avoids expensive optimization, and the computational cost analysis (Appendix C) shows training takes ~90s and inference overhead is negligible.

Evaluation is broad and generally convincing: 3-5 LLMs across sizes, 7+ jailbreak attacks, 4 utility benchmarks, comparisons against relevant steering baselines (Surgical, Jailbreak Antidote, CAST, Circuit Breaker), an ablation with the raw refusal vector (RV) that isolates the trade-off, and comparison to refusal SFT with favorable cost.

The analysis goes beyond aggregate metrics: PCA visualizations of activation dynamics, L2-norm distributions of steering vectors, an explanation of why CAST collapses on math prompts, space-coverage (PEC) analysis, sensitivity to benign data size and null-space ratio, and importantly an adaptive white-box GCG evaluation showing robustness of the defense.
The appendix honestly probes failure modes of baselines and the paper's own sensitivity to data volume (Tables 14-15), which supports the claimed mechanism rather than only end results.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is limited: Lemma 1 (null space of H equals null space of HH^T) is a standard, near-trivial fact, and the overall method reduces to a learned linear map (essentially a linear benign/malicious discriminator composed with a fixed refusal vector). The repeated claims of 'theoretical grounding' and 'learnability' overstate what is straightforward linear algebra plus ridge regression; 'we novelly introduce learnability' also ignores existing learned steering methods (e.g., Hegazy et al., Sun et al.) that the paper itself cites.

A key vulnerability is underexplored: the defense fails if a malicious activation falls inside the span of benign training activations (then ∆h ≈ 0 and no steering occurs). The approach implicitly relies on linear separability of benign/malicious activations — the very assumption underlying the conditional-steering baselines the paper criticizes as heuristic. The relationship to and advantages over conditional steering in this adversarial setting deserve deeper analysis.

Hyperparameter choices raise concern: steering strength λ and the null-space ratio p% appear selected per model, and the sweeps in Appendix F.8.2/F.6 suggest tuning based on test performance; the selection protocol (validation-based or not) is not clearly stated.

Evaluation limitations: test sets are small (100 prompts per attack), results are single-run with no variance or significance testing, and DSR is judged by GPT-4o, a noisy evaluator (the Llama-Guard comparison in Appendix G usefully shows large label discrepancies, e.g., Cipher, which further underlines evaluation sensitivity).

The framing as a training-free steering method is somewhat blurred: AlphaSteer uses ~2,000 labeled malicious prompts (including WildGuardMix and JailbreakV-28K) at fitting time, giving it an informational advantage over some baselines; the fairness of comparisons would be clearer if baselines used equivalent data.
Only 7-9B open models are tested; the limitations section concedes results on larger and reasoning models are unknown, which narrows the claimed significance for deployment.

Presentation issues: duplicated/near-duplicate references (Ouyang 2022a/b, Zou 2023b/c, Pan 2025a/b, Liu 2025a-c), mislabeled cross-references (Appendix E.6 says 'Table 7 reports DSR' but shows Figure 7), typos ('novelly', 'inlcude'), and occasional overclaiming language that should be tempered.
